title: A temporal association between folic acid fortification and an increase in colorectal cancer rates may be illuminating important biological principles: a hypothesis
authors: Mason JB, Dickstein A, Jacques PF, Haggarty P, Selhub J, Dallal G, et al.
population: National colorectal cancer incidence data, United States and Canada, before and after folic acid fortification began in 1996 to 1998
funder: Grant support: U.S. Department of Agriculture, under agreement no. 58-1950-4-401, NCI K05 CA100048.
authorConflicts: J. Selhub has been a paid consultant to Merck-Eprova, which produces 5-methylfolic acid, and Pam Lab, LLC, which markets vitamin supplements; P. Haggarty is a member of the UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition; J.B. Mason has been a paid consultant to Wyeth Consumer Healthcare, a manufacturer of multivitamins.
result: Colorectal cancer incidence, previously falling, began to rise in 1996 in the USA and 1998 in Canada, peaked in 1998 and 2000, and continued to exceed the prefortification trend by 4 to 6 cases per 100,000 people, outside the 95% confidence limits of the prior linear trend in each country and in both sexes; changes in endoscopy rates did not appear to account for it. The authors state that the observations do not prove causality and hypothesise that fortification may have been wholly or partly responsible, by accelerating growth of existing neoplasms.
